title: Päivi Seppälä starts as project coordinator
content:
Päivi Seppälä starts as project coordinator in the project Epistemic Significance of Concepts. Päivi is responsible for project planning, budgeting and everyday administration of the project. Päivi's background is in philosophy of science, financial administration, and congress organizing. Päivi will defend her dissertation "Technologies of (anti-)discrimination: perspectives from the philosophy of science and technology" in January, 2027.

title: New article: Patient-derived heart cells reveal how cardiomyopathy mutations affect stretch response and GATA4 compound effects
content:
We used mechanical stretch to mimic the mechanical load experienced by heart muscle cells and examined how patient-derived cells respond to this stimulus and the experimental GATA4-targeted compound 3i-1262. We found distinct baseline gene expression and responses to stretch in cells carrying HCM- or DCM-associated variants, while the effects of 3i-1262 varied between genotypes. Our findings highlight the value of patient-derived cells for studying disease-related stress responses and evaluating experimental compounds.

title: Lucia Cerullo’s Elamite Metalworks, Part 2
content:
Dr. Lucia Cerullo is an archaeologist and art historian with a PhD in Asia, Africa, and the Mediterraneum from the University of Naples “L’Orientale”, in Italy. Her academic path began with a focus on Elamite epigraphy, explored in her Bachelor’s thesis on royal inscriptions from Persepolis. Over time, she developed a dual focus in archaeology and epigraphy, which she sees as essential in fully understanding ancient cultures. She has worked as an archaeologist in Italy, and held senior roles in fieldwork across Uzbekistan and Iran, including nearly seven years at the Iran National Museum in Tehran. Her expertise focuses on 1st Millenium BCE material culture, especially metal objects and pottery. 

What can we learn from studying these collections, and what kind of knowledge gap can we fill with that knowledge?

title: Lähitulevaisuudessa syöpähoito voidaan räätälöidä jokaisen yksilöllisen immuunipuolustuksen mukaan, tutkija uskoo
content:
With an estimated 1.8 million mortalities per year, lung cancer is the deadliest cancer in the world. It also affects young people and people who have never smoked. Typically, this cancer is detected after it has already spread. 

Assistant Professor Heidi Haikala’s research focuses on cancer immunity, or the ability of the body’s defence system to identify and destroy cancer cells, as well as cancer drug resistance and precision cancer therapies.  A key question is why cancer immunotherapies, or drugs that activate the patient’s immune system against cancer, respond in different ways in different people: some patients respond effectively, which means that the drug is working, while in others the same drug’s effectiveness is poor or non-existent. 

“Practically speaking, cancer is a failure of the human immune system. In the study of lung cancer drug resistance, we focus primarily on the whole body’s immune system. This has been a groundbreaking research avenue in lung cancer as well as many other cancers. We now have the appropriate tools at last,” Haikala says.

title: Kuudelle tutkimushankkeelle kaupallistamisrahoitus Business Finlandilta
content:
The University of Helsinki currently has 22 Business Finland‑funded research projects underway that are preparing the commercialisation of new innovations, with total Business Finland funding exceeding €13 million.

The Research to Business projects aim to ready research‑based inventions for the market, for example by licensing a newly patented technology or by establishing a related spinout company after the project phase.

The six R2B projects launched over the summer and early autumn are based on three campuses as follows:

Meilahti

  • ReBiont’s bacterial therapeutic aims to restore a healthy gut microbiota after recurring Clostridioides difficile infections causing severe, even life-threatening symptoms. The project is led by university researcher Reetta Satokari.
  • In the SansCoeliac collaboration project a novel immune response-modifying treatment is being developed for celiac disease. The project is led by university researcher Tobias Freitag from the Faculty of Medicine, together with Professor Robert Luxenhofer from the Faculty of Science.
  • Clearome Bio project develops cleaner single cell sequencing. The project is led by postdoctoral researcher Ceren Seref‑Vujaklija.

title: Helsingistä Bolognaan: Una Europan kansainvälinen tohtoriohjelma avasi uusia tapoja tarkastella Suomen historiaa
content:
Doctoral researcher Iisa Aaltonen explores the public memory culture of Finland’s Independence Day and is completing her dissertation at two universities within Una Europa’s Cultural Heritage doctoral programme. The programme has taken her on an exchange to Bologna and offered new perspectives on cultural heritage, academic practices and the analysis of Finnish history.

Iisa Aaltonen is a historian, with a Master of Arts degree from the University of Helsinki, and she has also completed a master’s degree in cultural policy at the University of Jyväskylä.

Aaltonen found her way to Una Europa’s international doctoral programme through a recommendation from her supervisor. What particularly interested her in the programme were its diverse perspectives on cultural heritage, the opportunity for international experiences and networks, and a broader view of the academic world.

title: Luonnontieteellisen museon Elämän historia -sali sulkeutuu tammikuussa – uusi näyttely avautuu loppuvuodesta 2028
content:
The Natural History Museum’s History of Life is one of the museum’s most popular exhibitions. However, the exhibition, completed in 2008, has long been in need of an update, as it is outdated both in terms of content and exhibition technology.

– The new exhibition will present evolution and the development of biodiversity in a more spectacular and tangible way than before. This is the museum’s most significant renewal project in years, says Sanna Vuori, Head of the Public Engagement Unit at the Finnish Museum of Natural History.

The dinosaurs Giganotosaurus carolinii and Shunosaurus lii in the History of Life exhibition have become familiar to many museum visitors over the years. They will remain in the new exhibition but will be joined by never-before-seen reconstructions of prehistoric animals. Among other things, a reconstruction of the otter-like early whale Ambulocetus natans is currently being built in the museum’s conservation facilities.

title: Southnord Artfest 2026: Roots en Route
content:
Plants have always travelled – with the wind, with animals and birds, with humans. They have been carried across oceans, taken from their habitats and replanted to serve trade and empire.

Roots en Route is a multi-sensory installation by four artists who will create a multi-sensory installation in dialogue with the greenhouses – examining rootedness and displacement; asking what grows where it was planted and what survives the crossing. The African plants that fill the greenhouses carry their own histories of movement and adaptation.

Camille Norment in collaboration with Sofia Jernberg create a soundscape drawing on the insects and birds of the plants' homelands. Toubab Holmes' site-specific scent installation traces the hidden journeys of plants through the extractive system of perfumery. Charmaine Watkiss visits the botanical legacies and healing traditions of her Caribbean ancestry through large-scale drawings of Plant Warriors. Together, the three works read the botanical garden as an archive of movement, and the plants in it as things that were carried, taken and made to travel.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.

title: Ny policy brief efterlyser åtgärder för att möta värmeböljorna i Östersjön
content:
Global warming is having a major impact on the Baltic Sea, both through rising average temperatures and through marine heatwaves becoming increasingly common. Between 1982 and 2023 alone, 189 marine heatwaves were recorded in the Baltic Sea, and in recent years some of the highest surface temperatures ever have been measured.

This has major consequences for marine life, according to researchers at CoastClim, who have summarised the issue in a new policy brief, primarily written by Norman Göbeler at the Tvärminne Zoological Station.

Species that are already living at the limits of their temperature tolerance are usually hardest hit by heatwaves and may lose a large proportion of their biomass, whilst other species may benefit. However, heatwaves also affect processes in the sea, which can have major consequences for the entire ecosystem.

- Marine heatwaves can exacerbate eutrophication from within and undermine the effectiveness of measures taken to reduce nutrient inputs into the sea. The increased metabolic rate of organisms can also boost the formation and release of greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide and methane, from coastal waters and sediments, the researchers write.

title: We are looking for two new postdoctoral researchers!
content:
The Research Council of Finland-funded project “the Epistemic Significance of Concepts” based at Theoretical Philosophy at the University of Helsinki invites applications for two (2) fixed-term Postdoctoral Researcher positions. The positions are for four years, starting in April 2027 (or later as agreed).  

Position description  

The positions belong to a research project “the Epistemic Significance of Concepts” led by Academy Professor Maria Lasonen. The project is funded by the Research Council of Finland. The project will work alongside another project on concepts funded by the European Research Council, but its aims are complementary to those of the ERC project. 

Conceptual resources are crucial from an epistemic perspective. Having the right concepts allows asking the right questions, formulating new hypotheses, and providing good explanations. New concepts are often needed for developing theories that systematize data and make accurate predictions. Good concepts are projectable, providing a sound basis for inductive reasoning. They enable communicating one’s own experiences and recognizing various forms of injustice. In short, concepts enable acquiring knowledge and understanding – whether about the subatomic world, moral reality, or our own social experiences – that is otherwise out of reach. And on the flipside: inapt concepts can result in widespread ignorance. This project aims to ask epistemological questions about concepts in an empirically informed way.

title: Lähes joka kolmannella urheilijalla on kohonnut LDL-kolesteroli
content:
When athletes eat less than their training requires, their energy intake is insufficient for both training and essential body functions. Relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) is a model that describes the harm that such a deficit causes both body and mind.

Relative energy deficiency may disrupt endocrine, bone and mental health, for example. Insufficient eating has also been associated with elevated levels of LDL cholesterol, which increases the risk of cardiovascular diseases. This link has been scarcely studied among athletes.

In her doctoral thesis, Doctoral Researcher Julia Voutilainen (née Silvennoinen) investigated whether deficient food intake is reflected in the cholesterol levels of Finnish adult athletes. The study participants were 582 national and world-class athletes. 

The link between low energy availability and cholesterol was weak, and was most evident in women practising what are known as weight-sensitive sports, which include gymnastics and long-distance running and consider a light body advantageous.
